evidence.label: Infinitely many closed geodesic images on every Riemannian sphere

headline: Claims every Riemannian metric on a sphere of any dimension has infinitely many geometrically distinct closed geodesics.
scope: Every smooth Riemannian metric, degenerate ones included, on the standard sphere Sⁿ with n ≥ 2, and on every closed three-manifold.
plain: A closed geodesic is a straightest path that loops back to where it began. A long-standing problem asks if every closed curved space has infinitely many of them with different shapes. For spheres, this was known in dimension two and for typical metrics in higher dimensions. This paper claims it for every metric on every sphere. It also deduces the same for every closed three-dimensional space.
doesNot: This does not count how many closed geodesics there are up to a given length. It does not settle the problem for all closed manifolds. It has no Lean check.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: George Birkhoff, minimax construction of closed geodesics on spheres
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims the sphere case of a central problem on closed geodesics, including all degenerate metrics, and settles dimension three.

explanation:
Take an ellipsoid with half-axes 1, 1.01 and 1.02, a slightly squashed ball. Cut it by each of its three planes of symmetry. Each cut gives an ellipse, and each ellipse is a closed geodesic. A geodesic is a straightest path, and a closed one loops back smoothly to its start. Their lengths, computed numerically, are about 6.315, 6.346 and 6.377. A round sphere of radius 1 has great circles of length 2π, about 6.283. On a nearly round ellipsoid, Morse showed that every other closed geodesic is much longer. So finding infinitely many closed geodesics means finding longer and longer ones, and checking that they are really new.

A closed geodesic is prime if it goes around its loop once[2]. Two geodesics count as different only if their images, the sets of points they pass through, differ[3]. Going around an old loop twice gives nothing new. The closed-geodesic problem asks whether every closed curved space of dimension at least two has infinitely many different ones[4].

On spheres, this was hard. For many spaces, the topology of the space of all loops forces infinitely many geodesics. Spheres are too simple for that test to work[5]. The two-sphere case follows from work of Bangert with Franks or Hingston[6]. In higher dimensions, Rademacher proved it for typical, strongly bumpy metrics[7]. But a limit of typical metrics need not keep distinct images[8]. Others found an error in Klingenberg's claimed general proof. The paper points to two unsupported steps in a later claimed proof by Charles[9].

The paper claims the full sphere case. Every smooth metric on the sphere of any dimension n ≥ 2 has infinitely many prime closed geodesics with different images[1]. The same holds for every closed three-dimensional space, using Perelman's theorem and a result of Rademacher and Taimanov[10]. The proof argues by contradiction. Suppose only finitely many images exist. The obstacle is temporary classes, loop shapes that appear below some length and later disappear[11]. The paper bounds how many there can be. Then the symmetry of reflecting loops and shifting them by half a period gives a contradiction[12].

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The proof relies on string topology and delicate filtered homology estimates. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds: it would settle the sphere case and dimension three of a central problem. The proof is technical, and the paper itself notes gaps in two earlier claimed proofs. There is no Lean check or published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: A straightest possible path on a curved space.
A geodesic that returns smoothly to its starting point and direction.
A closed geodesic that goes around its loop once, not several times.
A rule for measuring lengths and angles at every point of a space.
A typical metric whose closed geodesics are all, in a precise sense, non-degenerate.
The space of all closed loops in a given space.
